vignette: When 24-year-old Miguel Ramirez-an energetic QA engineer from a modest family in Austin-was driving home after a long shift, a sudden mechanical failure sent his car into a collision with a delivery truck on the highway. The impact shattered his windshield, the airbags deployed, and for a fleeting second he saw the driver of the truck's face, pale and frightened, before the world slid into a dizzying blur. He survived, but the event left an indelible scar. Later, as he walked home, he felt a cold rush of panic, his heart hammering against his ribs, and he wondered why the universe had allowed this to happen to him. In the days that followed, conversations about accidents at work or with friends triggered that same surge of dread. Every time a coworker mentioned a recent crash on the radio, Miguel's throat tightened, and he felt the phantom shock of the day's impact flash before his eyes. These crash discussions stirred a wave of dissociation; Miguel began to feel as if the world was a movie-unreal, detached, a mere observation rather than participation. When a news report about a similar incident aired, the images of shattered glass and broken lives seemed to replay inside his mind, flooding him with a sense of impending doom. Miguel's responses to these triggers became increasingly automatic. When the memory of the crash floated up during a meeting, he would immediately think, "What if I had known? What if I could have stopped it?" The counterfactual thinking-imagining alternate outcomes-filled his thoughts and made him feel guilty. He began to avoid any situation where police might be involved, such as refusing to report the minor fender-bender that happened on his commute the following week. At the same time, he shut himself off from media: the news cable remained dark, and he refrained from reading online articles that described other accidents. These avoidance behaviors grew more pronounced each day. He avoided police, avoided media, and his counterfactual thoughts spiraled, leaving him exhausted. The very same triggers that provoked avoidance also sharpened Miguel's negative appraisals. Each crash discussion reminded him of his perceived failure to protect the people in the delivery truck, a haunting memory that "I should have done more." The sense that he was powerless to shield others from harm gnawed at his sense of agency. He developed a belief that "you can never know who will harm you," and his worldview darkened with the conviction that "nothing good can happen to me anymore." These appraisals, born from the relentless reliving of the crash, fed back into his avoidance: the more he feared harm and believed he was destined for misfortune, the more he clung to the counterfactual musings and the avoidance of police and media, hoping to preclude any chance of a new disaster. Miguel's job as a QA engineer had become a minefield of potential triggers. The QA team's routine meetings involved reviewing crash test data, and even discussing hypothetical product failures felt like a threat. When he watched a webinar on transportation safety at home, the screen's images made his heart race. The persistent feeling of detachment and the compulsive urge to avoid any "risk" situation-whether that meant refusing to speak about the crash or shunning a simple traffic report-began to erode his professional relationships. A senior colleague noticed Miguel's distant demeanor and suggested he take a leave of absence, but Miguel feared that stepping away would mean abandoning his responsibility to others, a fear that clung to him like a second injury. It was a night of relentless anxiety, sitting alone with the television dark, when Miguel realized he could no longer bear the weight of living in constant threat of the next crash. He could not keep pretending that his life was normal. The culmination of dissociative episodes, counterfactual rumination, avoidance of police and media, and the deep-seated negative beliefs that he had failed to protect others and that nothing good could come his way, left him exhausted, isolated, and desperate for relief. The day he finally walked into the clinic, his throat felt tight, his hands shook, and his thoughts were a tangled web of guilt and fear. He was terrified of another accident, but also hopeful that someone might help him untangle the knot of thoughts that had bound him since that fateful night on the highway.
